channel.title: Pugalenthi Magendran | Blog
channel.description: Thoughts on AI, ML, and building things that work.

item.title: TSMC's Capex Became the AI Industrial Plan
item.description: TSMC's 2026 capex is not just foundry spending. It is the industrial buildout behind AI compute across 2nm, 3nm, CoWoS, SoIC, advanced packaging and HPC capacity.

item.title: The Package Became the Computer
item.description: Advanced packaging moved from a back-end detail to the main AI scaling layer. CoWoS, HBM, SoIC, chiplets, hybrid bonding and die-to-die IO now matter as much as transistor scaling.

item.title: AWS Turned the CPU Into Cloud Infrastructure
item.description: Graviton3 was not just an Arm CPU. It showed AWS using Nitro, chiplets, custom storage, packaging and server design to turn the CPU into a fleet-level cloud economics weapon.

item.title: The EUV Materials War Behind AI Chips
item.description: ASML gets the attention, but EUV scaling also depends on photoresist, coaters, developers, dry resist, MOR, etch and defect control. The hidden battle is turning scarce EUV photons into high-yield wafers.

item.title: Intel Bet the Farm. Now It Has to Prove the Foundry
item.description: Intel's 2021 turnaround bet was necessary, but 2026 is the proof phase. 18A is in production, foundry losses are real, expansion is being disciplined, and Intel must earn external foundry trust.

item.title: Qualcomm's Modem-to-Antenna Moat
item.description: Qualcomm's ultraBAW filters were never just a component story. They were part of a broader modem-to-antenna strategy across RFFE, 5G, Wi-Fi 7, automotive, IoT and future wireless systems.

item.title: The Node Race Became a System Race
item.description: TSMC's 3nm delay was an early sign that node transitions were getting harder. In 2026, the foundry race is about more than 2nm: EUV, backside power, packaging, HBM, yield, customer trust, and AI-scale capacity.

item.title: The EUV Throughput Bottleneck
item.description: EUV source power was a bottleneck in 2021. By 2026, ASML improved throughput, High-NA readiness, and source power, but AI chip scaling still depends on more photons, uptime, and lower cost per wafer.

item.title: The Foundry That Quit Moore's Law Found a Second Life
item.description: GlobalFoundries did not become the next TSMC. But RF SOI, FD-SOI, silicon photonics, secure supply, automotive, defense, and AI data-center interconnects made its specialty foundry strategy far more important by 2026.

item.title: China's Silicon Carbide Bet: From Subsidy Boom to Overcapacity War
item.description: China built serious silicon carbide capacity, but SiC is not won by capex alone. The hard test is yield, reliability, automotive qualification, 8-inch manufacturing, and profitability through overcapacity.

item.title: The A15 Die Shot That Predicted Apple Silicon's Future
item.description: Apple's A15 looked weak if judged only by CPU gains. But the die shot showed Apple moving silicon budget into cache, GPU, neural compute, ISP, media, and system-level efficiency.

item.title: The Reliability Layer Behind AI Hardware
item.description: As AI processors, silicon photonics, silicon carbide devices, and advanced packages become more expensive, burn-in and reliability screening become critical infrastructure.

item.title: The Memory Oligopoly Became AI's Toll Booth
item.description: In 2021, Micron said it would not add DRAM or NAND wafers. In 2026, AI turned memory supply discipline into a bottleneck across HBM, server DRAM, NAND, and enterprise SSDs.

item.title: China's NAND Breakout Was Delayed, Not Defeated
item.description: YMTC did not create the NAND apocalypse on schedule. Export controls delayed it, AI demand absorbed it, and domestic equipment constraints reshaped it. But China's NAND breakout is still reshaping the global memory market.

item.title: The Boring Back-End of AI
item.description: The AI boom is not only about GPUs, HBM, EUV and CoWoS. Kulicke & Soffa shows why semiconductor back-end assembly, bonding, packaging and interconnects matter more than most people realize.

item.title: Apple Silicon After the CPU Era
item.description: In 2021, Apple's A15 looked like a warning sign. In 2026, the verdict is clearer: CPU gains slowed, but Apple moved the battleground to GPU, Neural Engine, memory, thermals, and the whole chip.

item.title: The Package Escaped the Wafer
item.description: How Applied Materials' 600mm panel-level packaging bet aged into the AI mega-package race, as CoWoS expands, HBM counts rise, glass substrates emerge, and the package becomes the scaling surface.

item.title: The Dead-Zone Layer
item.description: How the iPhone satellite rumor evolved into a real battle over low-bandwidth dead-zone connectivity across Apple, Amazon, Globalstar, Starlink, T-Mobile, carriers, 3GPP NTN, and FCC SCS.

item.title: The Vehicle Compute Backbone
item.description: Why NXP's 2021 Samsung-rumor story aged into a cleaner thesis about software-defined vehicles, zonal architecture, secure connectivity, edge AI, and the embedded layers that make intelligent machines work.

item.title: The Open ISA Talent Bet
item.description: Why Rivos shows that high-performance RISC-V is not about free cores, but elite CPU teams, full-stack software, memory architecture, and hyperscaler control.

item.title: The Architecture Gatekeeper
item.description: Why Arm China shows that in semiconductor IP, losing control over the distribution channel can become almost as serious as losing control over the technology itself.

item.title: The Custom AI Hardware Trap
item.description: Why Tesla Dojo showed that custom AI hardware is not won by impressive silicon alone, but by memory balance, software, interconnect, packaging, cooling, power delivery, and economics.

item.title: The Package Became the Computer
item.description: How Tesla Dojo showed that AI scaling is not just about faster chips, but package-scale integration, bandwidth, SRAM locality, power delivery, cooling, software, and rack-level systems.

item.title: The Back-End Bottleneck
item.description: Why Kulicke & Soffa's wire-bonder cycle is becoming a broader story about AI packaging, memory interconnect, thermo-compression bonding, hybrid bonding, and power semiconductor assembly.

item.title: The Wafer-Scale Training Bet
item.description: How Tesla's Dojo showed that AI scaling is not just about faster chips, but packaging, interconnect, memory, power delivery, cooling, and software.

item.title: The Semiconductor Substitution Ladder
item.description: Why China's chip-tool localization is real in cleaning, etch, deposition, CMP, and mature nodes, but still hits the hardest walls in lithography, photoresist, metrology, and advanced-node process integration.

item.title: The Power Efficiency Layer
item.description: Why Power Integrations is no longer just an ESG semiconductor story, but a hidden power-conversion layer for GaN, EVs, grids, battery storage, industrial systems, and 800 VDC AI factories.

item.title: The Foundry Trust Test
item.description: Why Intel's foundry comeback will not be proven by logos, evaluations, or packaging wins, but by committed external wafer volume.

item.title: The Android Flagship Breakout
item.description: How MediaTek moved from cheap-chip stigma to TSMC-node flagship, on-device AI, Smart Edge, automotive, and cloud AI ASIC ambitions.

item.title: The Bubble That Became Infrastructure
item.description: Why Nvidia's 2021 overvaluation story aged half right: crypto, gaming, and stock-split speculation faded, but the AI factory platform became real.

item.title: The AI Chip Software Wall
item.description: Why Graphcore's IPU shows that great silicon is not enough to beat Nvidia: AI hardware is a full-stack war of CUDA, kernels, frameworks, benchmarks, cloud access, trust, and capital.

item.title: The Fab That Outlived 3D XPoint
item.description: How Micron's failed 3D XPoint memory fab became Texas Instruments' 300mm analog and embedded semiconductor supply-chain weapon.

item.title: The Wafer-Scale Latency Bet
item.description: Why Cerebras is betting that the fastest path for inference and scientific AI is not more distributed complexity, but fewer chip boundaries.

item.title: The GAA Credibility Test
item.description: Why Samsung Foundry's 2nm comeback is about trust, not transistor marketing: from 3GAE delays to SF2, HBM base dies, advanced packaging, and the race to become TSMC's credible alternative.

item.title: The AI-Native Network
item.description: How Qualcomm's 5G infrastructure bet evolved into the AI-native network: private 5G, edge AI, Open RAN acceleration, positioning, AI-RAN, and 6G.

item.title: The Networked AI Bet
item.description: Why Tenstorrent is attacking Nvidia with open software, RISC-V IP, Ethernet-native scale-out, and switch-light AI systems rather than simply building a bigger GPU.

item.title: The Foundry Toll Road
item.description: Why TSMC's pricing power got stronger in the AI era: customers are buying performance-per-watt, CoWoS capacity, HBM integration, yield, scale, and trust.

item.title: The Clinic-on-Wrist Reality Check
item.description: Why Rockley's clinic-on-wrist vision was directionally right but early, and why non-invasive glucose and continuous biomarkers remain one of the hardest problems in wearable health.

item.title: The Other Leading Edge
item.description: Why GlobalFoundries still matters in an AI world without chasing 2nm: silicon photonics, RF-SOI, FD-SOI, GaN, eMRAM, and specialty manufacturing. TSMC dominates the logic frontier. GF is trying to own selected specialty frontiers.

item.title: The Inference Efficiency War
item.description: How Qualcomm is turning Cloud AI 100's edge-inference DNA into AI200 and AI250 rack-scale infrastructure for cost-per-token AI serving. Training gets headlines. Inference gets the bill.

item.title: When AI Runs Out of Copper
item.description: Why AI factories are hitting data-movement limits, and why optical I/O, co-packaged optics, Intel photonics, Nvidia networking, Broadcom switches, and TSMC COUPE matter. The race to replace copper with light has begun.

item.title: The Custom Silicon Flywheel
item.description: How Google's Argos VCU became the blueprint for hyperscaler custom silicon, from video acceleration to Axion CPUs, Ironwood TPUs, Meta MSVP, AWS Trainium, and Microsoft Maia. The cloud is becoming a portfolio of domain-specific machines.

item.title: Nvidia's Earnings Quality Test
item.description: From crypto GPUs in 2021 to AI capex in 2026, the real question is whether Nvidia's explosive data-center revenue turns into durable utilization and customer cash flow. The numbers are real. The question is who ultimately pays for the AI buildout.

item.title: The AI Memory Tax
item.description: How AI servers are repricing DRAM and NAND, squeezing smartphones, PCs, and low-end consumer electronics, and splitting the old semiconductor cycle. AI infrastructure is booming while consumer electronics absorbs the cost.

item.title: The Boring Back-End Boom
item.description: Why mature nodes, wirebonding, power modules, OSATs, and semiconductor back-end equipment are becoming strategic again. AI made the front-end famous. The back-end is where every chip becomes a product.

item.title: The Density Illusion
item.description: Why Apple's A14 exposed the gap between theoretical transistor density and real chip density, and why AI-era scaling now depends on SRAM, memory bandwidth, packaging, power, and architecture. Moore's Law did not die. It became a system problem.

item.title: The Modem-to-Antenna War
item.description: How Apple is taking apart Qualcomm's modem-RF moat, from the iPhone 12 mmWave antenna decision to the Apple C1 modem. Qualcomm still has the best complete engine. Apple is trying to own the car.

item.title: Nvidia Didn't Buy Arm. It Built the AI Factory Anyway.
item.description: How Nvidia failed to buy Arm but still built the CPU-GPU-DPU-networking-software stack behind the modern AI factory. The acquisition failed. The strategy did not.

item.title: MediaTek and the Fragmented Compute War
item.description: How MediaTek moved from Huawei-substitution thesis to a broader role in flagship phones, edge AI, automotive platforms, and custom data-center ASICs. In 2020, the question was who supplies Huawei. In 2026, the question is who supplies compute.

item.title: The Dry Resist War
item.description: Why Lam's Aether dry resist matters for EUV, High-NA lithography, DRAM, HBM, and AI-era chipmaking. EUV exposed the wafer. The resist has to do the rest.

item.title: The AI Memory Wall
item.description: Why DRAM, HBM, advanced packaging, and semicap became central to the AI infrastructure race. The AI boom is usually described as a GPU shortage. That is only half true. The deeper bottleneck is memory.

item.title: The Prompt Is Not Infrastructure
item.description: Prompts are instructions, not controls. As AI agents gain access to tools, private data, and external actions, trustworthy AI will require permissions, sandboxes, logs, and real infrastructure.

item.title: The Interface Coup
item.description: AI will not merely replace search. It may replace the interface layer. When assistants become the front door, apps become callable infrastructure and distribution moves from visibility to permission.

item.title: The Memory Moat
item.description: The next AI moat may not be the best model. It may be memory: the accumulated context that makes an assistant feel like it knows you. When AI remembers who you are becoming, switching tools becomes harder.

item.title: The Model Monoculture
item.description: What happens when millions of people think, write, code, research, and decide through the same few AI models? The danger is not only wrong answers. It is correlated cognition.

item.title: Liability Laundering
item.description: AI agents will not just answer questions. They will act across systems, tools, data, and customers. The hidden danger is liability laundering: humans remain responsible while practical control moves elsewhere.

item.title: The Free Intelligence Trap
item.description: Free AI is not just the next ad-supported product. Search monetized what people wanted. Social monetized who they were. AI may monetize the moment before they decide.

item.title: The Cheap Code Era
item.description: AI will automate coding before it can own software. The cheap code era is here, but the expensive part of software is moving from syntax to systems, judgment, verification, security, and accountability.

item.title: Yann LeCun's Billion-Dollar Bet: Intelligence Beyond the Next Token
item.description: LeCun's argument is not that LLMs are useless. It is that real intelligence may require world models that predict consequences, plan actions, and understand reality beyond text.

item.title: The Boiling Frog Economy
item.description: How AI quietly breaks the ladder before it breaks the job market. The danger is not that some jobs disappear. It is that the first rung disappears first.

item.title: The title was wrong. That's what made it historic.
item.description: Everyone remembers 'Attention Is All You Need' as the attention paper. The real innovation was something later summaries under-emphasized, and it explains everything that came after.

item.title: There is no Alexander without Aristotle
item.description: On intelligence as infrastructure, why the education system was never designed for you, and what it took to understand the world on my own terms.
